`Did you know:` the aye-aye, a lemur from [Madagascar]{.hl}, finds insect larvae by [tapping]{.hl} on wood with its long, thin middle finger and listening for hollow tunnels. Then it gnaws a hole and hooks the larvae out with the same finger.

_Source: Duke Lemur Center_

## Who I am

I am Dr Massimiliano Canzi, [Max]{.hl} for short.

. . .

I studied linguistics in [Milan]{.hl} (BA), [Manchester]{.hl} (MA) and [York]{.hl} (MSc), and returned to [Manchester]{.hl} for my PhD.

. . .

I work on how listeners [perceive]{.hl} speech and how speakers [produce]{.hl} it, mostly with experiments and quantitative methods. Other interests: forensic speech science, and `R`.

## My research

Some of the questions I have worked on:

- [What PMN?]{.hl} Processing phonological mismatch in semantics-free speech perception
- Do the [somatic features]{.hl} of a speaker mediate how we perceive their voice?
- A quantitative analysis of the acoustic differences between [neutral]{.hl} and [loud]{.hl} speech

## Who are you?

Tell us briefly:

- Your [name]{.hl} and your [programme]{.hl}
- The [data]{.hl} you work with, or would like to work with
- Your experience with `R`: none, some, lots
- One thing you would like to [take away]{.hl} from this course

# The course

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` aye-ayes have [incisors that never stop growing]{.hl}, like a rodent's. No other primate has them.

_Source: Duke Lemur Center_
:::

## How the course works

- [Lecture]{.hl}, Fridays at 11:45: new concepts, and the code that goes with them
- [Tutorial]{.hl}, Wednesdays at 13:30: you practise, with help at hand
- [Office hours]{.hl}, Fridays 10:00 to 11:30, by appointment
- [Ilias]{.hl}: announcements, homework and submissions

## Assessment

| Component | Weight |
|---|---|
| [Final assignment]{.hl} | 90% |
| [Homework]{.hl}: four of the five exercises count | 10% |

. . .

The homework exercises are short, a few questions each, and practise what we covered in class.

## The final assignment

You analyse a set of [linguistic data]{.hl} and write it up as a scientific report of about [3000 words]{.hl}, in the style of an experimental paper.

. . .

You hand in [one file]{.hl} that contains the text of your paper alongside the code of your analysis. Anyone who opens it can rerun your analysis and get the same numbers.

## Your own work

- The [text]{.hl} and the [code]{.hl} you submit must be your own
- [Cite]{.hl} every source you build on: papers, books, tutorials, code you adapt
- If in doubt, [ask]{.hl} before you submit

. . .

As The Smiths warn in _Cemetry Gates_ (1986): plagiarism tends to get noticed.

## Dissertations

I can supervise up to [two dissertations]{.hl} per semester as first supervisor, and up to [two]{.hl} as second supervisor.

. . .

If you would like to write a quantitative dissertation, get in touch [early]{.hl}.

## Slides and materials

The slides are written in [R Markdown]{.hl} and shown with `reveal.js`. Each week you get:

- the [slides]{.hl} (.html)
- the [code]{.hl} behind them (.Rmd)
- the [homework]{.hl} exercises

. . .

Open the .Rmd in RStudio and run it yourself: every number, table and plot on the slides comes from that code. Slides and code are also online, at `github.com/mcanzi/ws26_statistics`.

## The book

Winter, B. (2019). _Statistics for linguists: An introduction using R_. Routledge.

. . .

- Written [for linguists]{.hl}, with linguistic data throughout
- Uses `R` and the `tidyverse`, like this course
- Builds everything around the [linear model]{.hl}

# Getting started

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the aye-aye is the world's largest [nocturnal primate]{.hl}, at 2.5 to 2.8 kg. In parts of Madagascar many people see it as a bad omen (_fady_) that must be killed on sight.

_Source: Duke Lemur Center_
:::

## Software

You need two free programs:

1. `R`, the language itself. Download it from [CRAN](https://cloud.r-project.org/)
2. `RStudio`, the program you write and run R code in. Download it from [Posit](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html)

. . .

RStudio needs R to work, so install [R first]{.hl}.

## RStudio at a glance

<div style="background: var(--understory); border-left: 3px solid var(--hornbill); border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.6em 0.8em;"><strong>Console</strong><br>Where R runs your code and prints results. Code here is not saved.</div>

## Install the packages (once)

Type this in the RStudio `Console`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "palmerpenguins", "swirl"))
```

. . .

Check that everything worked:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
R.version.string          # your version of R
packageVersion("dplyr")   # should be 1.2.0 or newer
```

. . .

You [install]{.hl} a package once. You [load]{.hl} it with `library()` in every session.

# First steps in R

## Hello, world

```{r}
print("Hello, world!")
```

. . .

R is also a calculator:

```{r}
2 + 2
10 / 4
2 ^ 3
(3 + 2) * 4
```

. . .

Brackets work as in maths: without them, `3 + 2 * 4` gives `r 3 + 2 * 4`.

## Your first script

Code typed in the `Console` is gone once you close RStudio. Write it in a [script]{.hl} instead: _File > New File > R Script_.

. . .

```{r}
# everything after a hash is a comment: R ignores it
2 + 2   # comments can also follow code
```

. . .

Run the current line with `Ctrl + Enter` (`Cmd + Enter` on a Mac). Save the script, and you can rerun the whole analysis tomorrow.

## Storing values

`<-` stores a value in an [object]{.hl} (read it as "gets"):

```{r}
x <- 2 * 3
x
x + 1
```

. . .

- The object now appears in your `Environment`
- Names are [case sensitive]{.hl}: `x` and `X` are two different objects
- Names cannot start with a number or contain spaces: `word_freq` works, [word freq]{.hl} does not

## Vectors

`c()` combines values into a `vector`. Arithmetic works on every element at once:

```{r}
ages <- c(23, 31, 19, 45)
ages * 12
mean(ages)
```

. . .

Sequences of numbers:

```{r}
1:10
seq(0, 100, by = 25)
```

## Indexing

Square brackets pick out [elements]{.hl} by position:

```{r}
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
x[1]
x[2:4]
x[-1]          # everything except the first
```

. . .

Or by a [condition]{.hl}:

```{r}
x[x > 15]
```

## Logical vectors

A comparison returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each element:

```{r}
x > 15
```

. . .

`TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, so you can count and take proportions:

```{r}
sum(x > 15)    # how many?
mean(x > 15)   # what proportion?
```

. . .

Comparisons: `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`

## Text and categories

Text goes in `"quotes"`: a `character` vector.

```{r}
words <- c("cat", "dog", "cat", "bird", "cat")
table(words)
```

. . .

A `factor` stores categories, with a fixed set of `levels`:

```{r}
animal <- factor(words)
levels(animal)
```

. . .

Levels are sorted [alphabetically]{.hl} by default: this matters later.

## Data frames

A [data frame]{.hl} is a table whose columns are vectors of equal length:

```{r}
d <- data.frame(word = c("cat", "dog", "bird"),
                freq = c(120, 95, 30))
d
```

. . .

```{r}
d$freq          # one column
d[2, ]          # second row, all columns
```

## Functions and arguments

A function takes [arguments]{.hl} inside its brackets. Name them to make code readable:

```{r}
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

. . .

`NA` marks a missing value. Most summaries return `NA` if one is present, unless you say otherwise:

```{r}
mean(c(4, NA, 8))
mean(c(4, NA, 8), na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Getting help

- `?mean` opens the help page for `mean()`: read the [Arguments]{.hl}, and run the [Examples]{.hl} at the bottom
- Copy an [error message]{.hl} into a search engine: someone has almost always seen it before
- Ask in the [tutorial]{.hl}, or in office hours

. . .

R and its packages are written by researchers. Cite them in your work:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
citation()                 # how to cite R
citation("tidyverse")      # how to cite a package
```

## `swirl`

`swirl` teaches you R, inside R. Its interactive lessons range from the basics to modelling, and some of your homework will use them ([swirlstats.com](https://swirlstats.com/students.html)).

. . .

You installed it already. To start a lesson:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(swirl)
swirl()
```

The first time, `swirl` asks you to choose and install a course.

. . .

Inside a lesson: `bye()` quits and saves your progress, `skip()` skips a question, `main()` goes back to the menu.

## The `tidyverse`

The `tidyverse` is a collection of R packages, created by [Hadley Wickham](https://hadley.nz/) and colleagues, for importing, reshaping and plotting data.

. . .

It replaces many base R functions with alternatives that are easier to [write]{.hl}, [read]{.hl} and [reproduce]{.hl}. Think of it as a [dialect]{.hl} of R, with base R as the standard variety.

. . .

We start using it next week. It builds on everything you saw today: vectors, data frames and functions.

# Statistics

## Objective or subjective?

Discuss:

- Two researchers analyse the [same data]{.hl}. Do they reach the [same conclusion]{.hl}?
- Which decisions in an analysis are [yours]{.hl} to make?

## Objective or subjective?

Coretta et al. (2023) gave [one speech production data set]{.hl} and [one research question]{.hl} to [46 teams]{.hl} of analysts.

. . .

- The teams reported [substantially different]{.hl} effect sizes and interpretations
- Neither prior beliefs nor expertise explained the differences

. . .

Statistics does not remove [choices]{.hl}. It makes them [explicit]{.hl}, so others can check them.

## What you will learn

By the end of the course you will be able to:

- [describe]{.hl} and [plot]{.hl} linguistic data in R
- build, interpret and check [regression models]{.hl}, from simple linear models to mixed effects and logistic regression
- [report]{.hl} an analysis so that others can follow it and reproduce it

Let's open `RStudio` and try all of this ourselves.
